If the set of all possible values of $a$ is $R-[\alpha,\beta]$ , then $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $\frac{x^{2}}{f(a^{2}+7a+3)}+\frac{y^{2}}{f(3a+15)}=1$ represent an ellipse with major axis along $y$ -axis, where $f$ is a strictly decreasing positive function on $R$ . If the set of all possible values of $a$ is $R-[\alpha,\beta]$ , then $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Since the ellipse has its major axis along the $y$ -axis, the denominator under $y^{2}$ must be bigger than the denominator under $x^{2}$ . So we need $f(3a+15)>f(a^{2}+7a+3).$ Given that $f$ is a strictly decreasing positive function, a bigger function value happens when the input is smaller. So, $3a+15<a^{2}+7a+3.$ Bring all terms to one side: $a^{2}+7a+3-3a-15>0$ $a^{2}+4a-12>0.$ Complete the square: $a^{2}+4a-12=(a+2)^{2}-16.$ So the inequality becomes $(a+2)^{2}-16>0 \Rightarrow (a+2)^{2}>16.$ Taking square roots, $|a+2|>4 \Rightarrow a+2>4\text{or}a+2<-4.$ So, $a>2\text{or}a<-6.$ That means the allowed values are $a \in R-[-6,2].$ Hence, $\alpha=-6$ and $\beta=2$ . Therefore, $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(-6)^{2}+(2)^{2}=36+4=40.$

questions.question_text: Let an ellipse $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ , $a<b$ , pass through the point (4, 3) and have eccentricity $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ . Then the length of its latus rectum is :
questions.question_html:
Let an ellipse $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ , $a<b$ , pass through the point (4, 3) and have eccentricity $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ .

Then the length of its latus rectum is :
questions.explanation_text: Since $a<b$ , the major axis is along the $y$ -axis. So for the ellipse $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1,$ we use the eccentricity formula $e=\sqrt{1-\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}}.$ Given $e=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3},$ so $e^{2}=\frac{5}{9}.$ Hence, $1-\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}=\frac{5}{9}$ which gives $\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}=1-\frac{5}{9}=\frac{4}{9}.$ Therefore, $a^{2}=\frac{4}{9}b^{2}.$ Now the ellipse passes through $(4,3)$ , so it satisfies the equation: $\frac{4^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{3^{2}}{b^{2}}=1.$ That is, $\frac{16}{a^{2}}+\frac{9}{b^{2}}=1.$ Substitute $a^{2}=\frac{4}{9}b^{2}$ : $\frac{16}{\frac{4}{9}b^{2}}+\frac{9}{b^{2}}=1.$ Simplifying, $16 \cdot \frac{9}{4b^{2}}+\frac{9}{b^{2}}=1$ $\frac{36}{b^{2}}+\frac{9}{b^{2}}=1$ $\frac{45}{b^{2}}=1$ so $b^{2}=45.$ Then $a^{2}=\frac{4}{9} \cdot 45=20.$ For an ellipse with major axis along the $y$ -axis, the length of latus rectum is $\frac{2a^{2}}{b}.$ So, $\text{Length of latus rectum}=\frac{2 \cdot 20}{\sqrt{45}}=\frac{40}{3\sqrt{5}}.$ Rationalising, $\frac{40}{3\sqrt{5}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{8\sqrt{5}}{3}.$ Therefore, the correct answer is $\frac{8\sqrt{5}}{3}$ So, Option D is correct.

$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1,$

$e=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3},$

$1-\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}=\frac{5}{9}$

which gives

$\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}=1-\frac{5}{9}=\frac{4}{9}.$

Therefore,

$a^{2}=\frac{4}{9}b^{2}.$

Now the ellipse passes through $(4,3)$ , so it satisfies the equation:

$\frac{4^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{3^{2}}{b^{2}}=1.$

That is,

$\frac{16}{a^{2}}+\frac{9}{b^{2}}=1.$

Substitute $a^{2}=\frac{4}{9}b^{2}$ :

$\frac{36}{b^{2}}+\frac{9}{b^{2}}=1$

$\frac{45}{b^{2}}=1$

For an ellipse with major axis along the $y$ -axis, the length of latus rectum is

Rationalising,

$\frac{40}{3\sqrt{5}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{8\sqrt{5}}{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\frac{8\sqrt{5}}{3}$

questions.question_text: If the points of intersection of the ellipses $x^{2}+2y^{2}-6x-12y+23=0$ and $4x^{2}+2y^{2}-20x-12y+35=0$ lie on a circle of radius $r$ and centre $(a,b)$ , then the value of $ab+18r^{2}$ is :
questions.question_html:
If the points of intersection of the ellipses $x^{2}+2y^{2}-6x-12y+23=0$ and

$4x^{2}+2y^{2}-20x-12y+35=0$ lie on a circle of radius $r$ and centre $(a,b)$ , then the

value of $ab+18r^{2}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the given ellipses be : $\begin{aligned} & S_{1} \equiv x^{2}+2y^{2}-6x-12y+23=0 \\ & S_{2} \equiv 4x^{2}+2y^{2}-20x-12y+35=0 \end{aligned}$ The equation of a curve passing through the intersection of these two ellipses is given by the family of curves $S_{1}+\lambda S_{2}=0$ : $(x^{2}+2y^{2}-6x-12y+23)+\lambda(4x^{2}+2y^{2}-20x-12y+35)=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $(1+4\lambda)x^{2}+(2+2\lambda)y^{2}-(6+20\lambda)x-(12+12\lambda)y+(23+35\lambda)=0$ Condition for circle: coefficient of $x^{2}=$ coefficient of $y^{2}$ $1+4\lambda=2+2\lambda$ $\Rightarrow$ $2\lambda=1$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}$ Substitute $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}$ : $3x^{2}+3y^{2}-16x-18y+\frac{81}{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $x^{2}+y^{2}-\frac{16}{3}x-6y+\frac{27}{2}=0$ $\begin{aligned} & 2g=-\frac{16}{3}⟹g=-\frac{8}{3} \\ & 2f=-6⟹f=-3 \\ & \text{Centre}(a,b)=(-g,-f)=(\frac{8}{3},3) \\ & a=\frac{8}{3},b=3 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & r^{2}=g^{2}+f^{2}-c \\ & r^{2}=(-\frac{8}{3})^{2}+(-3)^{2}-\frac{27}{2} \\ & r^{2}=\frac{64}{9}+9-\frac{27}{2} \\ & r^{2}=\frac{128+162-243}{18} \\ & r^{2}=\frac{47}{18} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & ab+18r^{2}=(\frac{8}{3})(3)+18(\frac{47}{18}) \\ & ab+18r^{2}=8+47=55 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the given ellipses be :

$\begin{aligned} & S_{1} \equiv x^{2}+2y^{2}-6x-12y+23=0 \\ & S_{2} \equiv 4x^{2}+2y^{2}-20x-12y+35=0 \end{aligned}$

The equation of a curve passing through the intersection of these two ellipses is given by the family of curves $S_{1}+\lambda S_{2}=0$ :

$(x^{2}+2y^{2}-6x-12y+23)+\lambda(4x^{2}+2y^{2}-20x-12y+35)=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $(1+4\lambda)x^{2}+(2+2\lambda)y^{2}-(6+20\lambda)x-(12+12\lambda)y+(23+35\lambda)=0$

Condition for circle: coefficient of $x^{2}=$ coefficient of $y^{2}$

$1+4\lambda=2+2\lambda$

$\Rightarrow$ $2\lambda=1$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}$

Substitute $\lambda=\frac{1}{2}$ :

$3x^{2}+3y^{2}-16x-18y+\frac{81}{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $x^{2}+y^{2}-\frac{16}{3}x-6y+\frac{27}{2}=0$

$\begin{aligned} & 2g=-\frac{16}{3}⟹g=-\frac{8}{3} \\ & 2f=-6⟹f=-3 \\ & \text{Centre}(a,b)=(-g,-f)=(\frac{8}{3},3) \\ & a=\frac{8}{3},b=3 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & r^{2}=g^{2}+f^{2}-c \\ & r^{2}=(-\frac{8}{3})^{2}+(-3)^{2}-\frac{27}{2} \\ & r^{2}=\frac{64}{9}+9-\frac{27}{2} \\ & r^{2}=\frac{128+162-243}{18} \\ & r^{2}=\frac{47}{18} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & ab+18r^{2}=(\frac{8}{3})(3)+18(\frac{47}{18}) \\ & ab+18r^{2}=8+47=55 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let A be the point (3, 0) and circles with variable diameter AB touch the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=36$ internally. Let the curve C be the locus of the point B. If the eccentricity of C is $e$ , then $72e^{2}$ is equal to ________.
questions.question_html: Let A be the point (3, 0) and circles with variable diameter AB touch the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=36$ internally. Let the curve C be the locus of the point B. If the eccentricity of C is $e$ , then $72e^{2}$ is equal to ________.
questions.explanation_text: Let the variable point be $B(ℎ,k)$ . We are told that the circle having $AB$ as diameter touches the fixed circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=36$ internally. If a circle has endpoints of a diameter at $A(3,0)$ and $B(ℎ,k)$ , then its equation is $(x-ℎ)(x-3)+(y-k)(y-0)=0$ Expanding this, we get $x^{2}+y^{2}-(ℎ+3)x-ky+3ℎ=0$ So, the centre of this circle is Centre $(\frac{ℎ+3}{2},\frac{k}{2})$ Now, the fixed circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=36$ has centre $C_{1}(0,0)$ and radius $R=6$ . The variable circle (with diameter $AB$ ) has radius equal to half of $AB$ , so $r=\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{(ℎ-3)^{2}+k^{2}})$ Since the two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres equals the difference of radii: $\therefore C_{1}C_{2}=|R-r|$ Here, $C_{2}(\frac{ℎ+3}{2},\frac{k}{2})$ . So, $\sqrt{(\frac{ℎ+3}{2})^{2}+(\frac{k}{2})^{2}}=|6-\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{(ℎ-3)^{2}+k^{2}})|$ On simplifying and writing the locus in terms of a general point $(x,y)$ (i.e., replacing $(ℎ,k)$ by $(x,y)$ ), we get $\sqrt{(x+3)^{2}+y^{2}}+\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}+y^{2}}=12$ This is the standard form of an ellipse: sum of distances from two fixed points (foci) is constant $=2a$ . So, $2a=12 \therefore a=6$ Comparing, the foci are $(-3,0)$ and $(3,0)$ . The distance between the foci is $6$ , so $2c=6$ . Using $c=ae$ , we write $2ae=6$ Substituting $a=6$ : $12e=6$ So, $e=\frac{1}{2}$ Finally, $\therefore 72e^{2}=72(\frac{1}{4})=18$

questions.question_html: Let $x=9$ be a directrix of an ellipse E , whose centre is at the origin and eccentricity is $\frac{1}{3}$ . Let $P(\alpha,0)$ , $\alpha>0$ , be a focus of E and AB be a chord passing through P . Then the locus of the mid point of AB is :
questions.explanation_text: Since the centre of the ellipse is at the origin and one directrix is $x=9$ , the major axis is along the $x$ -axis. Let the ellipse be $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ with eccentricity $e=\frac{1}{3}$ For an ellipse with major axis along the $x$ -axis, the directrices are $x= \pm \frac{a}{e}$ Given one directrix is $x=9$ , so $\frac{a}{e}=9$ Since $e=\frac{1}{3}$ , $a=9 \cdot \frac{1}{3}=3$ Also, $c=ae=3 \cdot \frac{1}{3}=1$ So the focus $P(\alpha,0)$ is $P=(1,0)$ Hence $\alpha=1$ . Now, $b^{2}=a^{2}(1-e^{2})=9(1-\frac{1}{9})=9 \cdot \frac{8}{9}=8$ Therefore the ellipse is $\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{8}=1$ Let the midpoint of chord $AB$ passing through the focus $(1,0)$ be $(ℎ,k)$ . For the ellipse $\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{8}=1$ the equation of the chord whose midpoint is $(ℎ,k)$ is given by the NCERT midpoint formula: $\frac{xx_{1}}{9}+\frac{yy_{1}}{8}=\frac{x_{1}^{2}}{9}+\frac{y_{1}^{2}}{8}$ So here the chord with midpoint $(ℎ,k)$ is $\frac{xℎ}{9}+\frac{yk}{8}=\frac{ℎ^{2}}{9}+\frac{k^{2}}{8}$ Since this chord passes through the focus $(1,0)$ , substitute $(x,y)=(1,0)$ : $\frac{ℎ}{9}=\frac{ℎ^{2}}{9}+\frac{k^{2}}{8}$ Multiply by $72$ : $8ℎ=8ℎ^{2}+9k^{2}$ So, $9k^{2}=8ℎ-8ℎ^{2}=8ℎ(1-ℎ)$ Replacing $(ℎ,k)$ by $(x,y)$ for the locus of the midpoint, we get $9y^{2}=8x(1-x)$ Hence the required locus is $9y^{2}=8x(1-x)$ So the correct option is A .

Since the centre of the ellipse is at the origin and one directrix is $x=9$ , the major axis is along the $x$ -axis.

Let the ellipse be

$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$

with eccentricity

$e=\frac{1}{3}$

$x= \pm \frac{a}{e}$

Given one directrix is $x=9$ , so

$\frac{a}{e}=9$

Since $e=\frac{1}{3}$ ,

$a=9 \cdot \frac{1}{3}=3$

Also,

$c=ae=3 \cdot \frac{1}{3}=1$

So the focus $P(\alpha,0)$ is

$P=(1,0)$

Hence $\alpha=1$ .

Now,

$b^{2}=a^{2}(1-e^{2})=9(1-\frac{1}{9})=9 \cdot \frac{8}{9}=8$

Therefore the ellipse is

$\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{8}=1$

Let the midpoint of chord $AB$ passing through the focus $(1,0)$ be $(ℎ,k)$ .

For the ellipse

$\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{8}=1$

the equation of the chord whose midpoint is $(ℎ,k)$ is given by the NCERT midpoint formula:

$\frac{xx_{1}}{9}+\frac{yy_{1}}{8}=\frac{x_{1}^{2}}{9}+\frac{y_{1}^{2}}{8}$

So here the chord with midpoint $(ℎ,k)$ is

$\frac{xℎ}{9}+\frac{yk}{8}=\frac{ℎ^{2}}{9}+\frac{k^{2}}{8}$

Since this chord passes through the focus $(1,0)$ , substitute $(x,y)=(1,0)$ :

$\frac{ℎ}{9}=\frac{ℎ^{2}}{9}+\frac{k^{2}}{8}$

Multiply by $72$ :

$8ℎ=8ℎ^{2}+9k^{2}$

So,

$9k^{2}=8ℎ-8ℎ^{2}=8ℎ(1-ℎ)$

Replacing $(ℎ,k)$ by $(x,y)$ for the locus of the midpoint, we get

$9y^{2}=8x(1-x)$

Hence the required locus is

$9y^{2}=8x(1-x)$

So the correct option is A.

questions.question_html: An ellipse has its center at $(1,-2)$ , one focus at $(3,-2)$ and one vertex at $(5,-2)$ . Then the length of its latus rectum is :
questions.explanation_text: Given Center of ellipse : $(1,-2)$ Focus : $(3,-2)$ Vertex : $(5,-2)$ The center, focus, and vertex all have the same $y$ -coordinate $(-2)$ , which means the major axis of the ellipse is horizontal (parallel to the $x$ -axis). Find $a$ (semi-major axis) Distance from center to vertex : $a=|5-1|=4$ Find $c$ (distance from center to focus) $c=|3-1|=2$ Find $b$ using ellipse relation $c^{2}=a^{2}-b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $2^{2}=4^{2}-b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 4=16-b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow b^{2}=12$ $\Rightarrow b=2\sqrt{3}$ Length of latus rectum For an ellipse : Length of latus rectum $=\frac{2b^{2}}{a}$ $=\frac{2(12)}{4}=6$

Given

  • Focus : $(3,-2)$

  • Vertex : $(5,-2)$

The center, focus, and vertex all have the same $y$ -coordinate $(-2)$ , which means the major axis of the ellipse is horizontal (parallel to the $x$ -axis).

Find $a$ (semi-major axis)

Distance from center to vertex :

$a=|5-1|=4$

Find $c$ (distance from center to focus)

$c=|3-1|=2$

Find $b$ using ellipse relation

$c^{2}=a^{2}-b^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $2^{2}=4^{2}-b^{2}$

$\Rightarrow 4=16-b^{2}$

$\Rightarrow b^{2}=12$

$\Rightarrow b=2\sqrt{3}$

Length of latus rectum

For an ellipse :

Length of latus rectum $=\frac{2b^{2}}{a}$

$=\frac{2(12)}{4}=6$

Given the ellipse $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ with $a>b$ , the eccentricity $e$ is given by the formula:

$e=\sqrt{1-(\frac{b}{a})^{2}}$

It is provided that the eccentricity $e$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ (given), so we can equate the two expressions for eccentricity:

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{1-(\frac{b}{a})^{2}}$

Squaring both sides to eliminate the square root gives:

$\frac{1}{2}=1-(\frac{b}{a})^{2}$

$(\frac{b}{a})^{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}$

$(\frac{b}{a})^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$b^{2}=7$

And since $a=b\sqrt{2}$ , we can find $a^{2}$ :

$a^{2}=(b\sqrt{2})^{2}$

$a^{2}=14$

Now we have an ellipse with $a^{2}=14$ and $b^{2}=7$ . The equation of a hyperbola similar to the given ellipse but with the terms subtracted is:

questions.explanation_text: Given curve, $9x^{2}+16y^{2}=144$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{y^{2}}{9}=1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{4^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{3^{2}}=1$ $\therefore$ a = 4 and b = 3 So, general point on the ellipse is $=(4cos\theta,3sin\theta)$ We know, Equation of tangent to a given ellipse at its point $(acos\theta,bsin\theta)$ is $\frac{xcos\theta}{a}+\frac{ysin\theta}{b}=1$ $\therefore$ Here equation of tangent at point $(4cos\theta,3sin\theta)$ is $\frac{xcos\theta}{4}+\frac{ysin\theta}{3}=1$ When this tangent cut's x axis then y = 0. $\therefore$ $\frac{xcos\theta}{4}+0=1$ $\Rightarrow x=4sec\theta$ $\therefore$ Point of intersection at x axis is $A(4sec\theta,0)$ . When this tangent cut's y axis then x = 0. $\therefore$ $0+\frac{ysin\theta}{3}=1$ $\Rightarrow y=3cosec\theta$ $\therefore$ Point of intersection at y axis is $B(0,3cosec\theta)$ $\therefore$ Length of AB $=\sqrt{(4sec\theta-0)^{2}+(0-3cosec\theta)^{2}}$ $=\sqrt{16sec^{2}\theta+9cosec^{2}\theta}$ $=\sqrt{16(1+tan^{2}\theta)+9(1+cot^{2}\theta)}$ $=\sqrt{25+16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta}$ We know, $AM \ge GM$ $\therefore$ $\frac{16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta}{2} \ge \sqrt{(16tan^{2}\theta)(9cot^{2}\theta)}$ $\Rightarrow 16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta \ge 2(4tan\theta)(3cot\theta)$ $\Rightarrow 16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta \ge 2 \times 4 \times 3$ $\Rightarrow 16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta \ge 24$ $\therefore$ $AB=\sqrt{25+16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta}$ $\ge \sqrt{25+24}$ $\ge \sqrt{49}$ $\ge 7$ $\therefore$ Minimum length of $AB=7$ .

Given curve,

$9x^{2}+16y^{2}=144$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{y^{2}}{9}=1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{4^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{3^{2}}=1$

$\therefore$ a = 4 and b = 3

So, general point on the ellipse is $=(4cos\theta,3sin\theta)$

We know,

Equation of tangent to a given ellipse at its point $(acos\theta,bsin\theta)$ is

$\frac{xcos\theta}{a}+\frac{ysin\theta}{b}=1$

$\therefore$ Here equation of tangent at point $(4cos\theta,3sin\theta)$ is

$\frac{xcos\theta}{4}+\frac{ysin\theta}{3}=1$

When this tangent cut's x axis then y = 0.

$\therefore$ $\frac{xcos\theta}{4}+0=1$

$\Rightarrow x=4sec\theta$

$\therefore$ Point of intersection at x axis is $A(4sec\theta,0)$ .

When this tangent cut's y axis then x = 0.

$\therefore$ $0+\frac{ysin\theta}{3}=1$

$\Rightarrow y=3cosec\theta$

$\therefore$ Point of intersection at y axis is $B(0,3cosec\theta)$

$\therefore$ Length of AB

$=\sqrt{(4sec\theta-0)^{2}+(0-3cosec\theta)^{2}}$

$=\sqrt{16sec^{2}\theta+9cosec^{2}\theta}$

$=\sqrt{16(1+tan^{2}\theta)+9(1+cot^{2}\theta)}$

$=\sqrt{25+16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta}$

We know, $AM \ge GM$

$\therefore$ $\frac{16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta}{2} \ge \sqrt{(16tan^{2}\theta)(9cot^{2}\theta)}$

$\Rightarrow 16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta \ge 2(4tan\theta)(3cot\theta)$

$\Rightarrow 16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta \ge 2 \times 4 \times 3$

$\Rightarrow 16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta \ge 24$

$\therefore$ $AB=\sqrt{25+16tan^{2}\theta+9cot^{2}\theta}$

$\ge \sqrt{25+24}$

$\ge \sqrt{49}$

$\ge 7$

$\therefore$ Minimum length of $AB=7$ .

questions.explanation_text: The given ellipse has the equation : $x^{2}+4y^{2}=36$ We can rewrite this as : $\frac{x^{2}}{6^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{(6/2)^{2}}=1$ This shows that it is an ellipse centered at (0,0) with semi-major axis a = 6 along the x-axis and semi-minor axis b = 3 along the y-axis. 4x2 + 9y2 = 36 and (2x)2 + (2y)2 = 31. Then the

square of the slope of the line L is __________.
questions.explanation_text: Tangent to the curve $\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{14}=1$ is $y=mx+\sqrt{9m^{2}+4}$ and equation of tangent to the curve $x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{31}{4}$ is $y=mx+\sqrt{\frac{31}{4}(1+m)^{2}}$ for common tangent $9m^{2}+4=\frac{31}{4}+\frac{31}{4}m^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{5}{4}m^{2}=\frac{15}{4}$ $\Rightarrow m^{2}=3$

questions.question_html: The ellipse $x^{2}+4y^{2}=4$ is inscribed in a rectangle aligned with the coordinate axex, which in turn is inscribed in another ellipse that passes through the point $(4,0)$ . Then the equation of the ellipse is :
questions.explanation_text: The given ellipse is $\frac{x^{2}}{4}+\frac{y^{2}}{1}=1$ So $A=(2,0)$ and $B=(0,1)$ If $PQRS$ is the rectangular in which it is inscribed, then $P=(2,1).$ Let $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ be the ellipse circumscribing the rectangular $PQRS$ . Then it passes through $P(2,1)$ $\therefore$ $\frac{4}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}=1...(a)$ Also, given that, it passes through $(4,0)$ $\therefore$ $\frac{16}{a^{2}}+0=1 \Rightarrow a^{2}=16$ $\Rightarrow b^{2}=4/3$ $[$ substituting $a^{2}=16$ in $eq^{n}(a)]$ $\therefore$ The required ellipse is $\frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{y^{2}}{4/3}=1$ or $x^{2}+12y^{2}=16$
questions.explanation_html:
The given ellipse is $\frac{x^{2}}{4}+\frac{y^{2}}{1}=1$

So $A=(2,0)$ and $B=(0,1)$

If $PQRS$ is the rectangular in which it is inscribed, then

$P=(2,1).$

Let $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$

be the ellipse circumscribing the rectangular $PQRS$ .

Then it passes through $P(2,1)$

$\therefore$ $\frac{4}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}=1...(a)$

Also, given that, it passes through $(4,0)$

$\therefore$ $\frac{16}{a^{2}}+0=1 \Rightarrow a^{2}=16$

$\Rightarrow b^{2}=4/3$ $[$ substituting $a^{2}=16$ in $eq^{n}(a)]$

$\therefore$ The required ellipse is $\frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{y^{2}}{4/3}=1$

or $x^{2}+12y^{2}=16$
